ready1_open_rewrite.title: PhysReason open-ended question
ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: In mountainous areas with continuous downhill sections, highways often have an additional "escape lane" on the outside of the main traffic lane, known as a runaway truck ramp, designed to allow vehicles that have lost control of their speed to safely decelerate away from the main traffic. A truck, after entering the downhill section, experienced brake failure due to continuous use of the brakes and entered the escape ramp at a speed of $42\mathrm{m/s}$. It then underwent uniformly decelerated linear motion with an acceleration magnitude of $12\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, coming to a complete stop just as it reached the top of the escape ramp. 1. The speed of the truck 2 seconds after entering the escape ramp; 2. How long should the escape ramp be at least?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: In mountainous areas with continuous downhill sections, highways often have an additional "escape lane" on the outside of the main traffic lane, known as a runaway truck ramp, designed to allow vehicles that have lost control of their speed to safely decelerate away from the main traffic. A truck, after entering the downhill section, experienced brake failure due to continuous use of the brakes and entered the escape ramp at a speed of $42\mathrm{m/s}$. It then underwent uniformly decelerated linear motion with an acceleration magnitude of $12\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^{2}$, coming to a complete stop just as it reached the top of the escape ramp. 1. The speed of the truck 2 seconds after entering the escape ramp; 2. How long should the escape ramp be at least?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: The image shows a scene of a branch-off lane/distress lane beside a section of highway, and the roadside sign reads “Distress lane”, indicating that this is an escape/distress lane for out-of-control vehicles to enter and slow down. The image itself does not give numerical information such as speed, acceleration, or length. Then reason: The problem text gives that the initial speed of the truck when entering the distress lane is v0 = 42 m/s, and it undergoes uniformly decelerated straight-line motion, with acceleration magnitude 12 m/s^2; therefore, taking the direction of motion as the positive direction, a = -12 m/s^2. 1. The speed 2 s after entering the distress lane: use the formula vt = v0 + at, substitute t = 2 s, obtaining vt = 42 + (-12)×2 = 42 - 24 = 18 m/s. 2. The minimum length of the distress lane: the truck just stops when reaching the top of the slope, and the final speed v = 0. Use the formula v^2 - v0^2 = 2as, substitute 0^2 - 42^2 = 2×(-12)×s, obtaining s = (0 - 1764)/(-24) = 73.5 m. Therefore the distress lane should be at least 73.5 m.

method.method_draft: First inspect the image: it shows a highway in a mountainous/roadside setting with a sign reading “Distress lane,” confirming that the scenario is a runaway/escape ramp, but it provides no numerical measurements. From the text, take the initial speed on entering the ramp as v0 = 42 m/s, the uniformly decelerating acceleration as a = -12 m/s^2, and the final speed at the top as v = 0. For part 1, apply the constant-acceleration velocity formula v_t = v0 + at at t = 2 s, giving v_t = 42 - 12×2 = 18 m/s. For part 2, apply the no-time kinematic equation v^2 - v0^2 = 2as with v = 0 and a = -12 m/s^2, then solve s = (0^2 - 42^2)/(2×(-12)) = 73.5 m. Therefore the ramp must be at least 73.5 m long.
